We have actively participated in and supported the work of the United Nations . We are a small country , but we have never been afraid to speak out about what is just and right . <p> New Zealand is also strongly committed to sustainable development at home and internationally , and supports the 2030 Agenda . <p> The principles behind the Sustainable Development Goals are embedded in New Zealand 's domestic policies . The Goals also provide a framework for our international development cooperation , especially in the Pacific , and other international engagement . <p> We often say that New Zealand is an egalitarian nation . However , there are areas in which we are falling short of our aspirations and our reputation , which I will discuss today . <p> New Zealand is founded on a partnership between Maori , the tangata whenua , indigenous people , of New Zealand and the Crown ( or Government ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ o Waitangi ( the Treaty of Waitangi ) , was signed . The intent was to formalise an enduring partnership between Maori and the Crown . The Treaty encompasses both individual and collective rights and provides a framework for the State to promote , protect and respect indigenous rights . <p> Today , the Treaty is recognised for its constitutional significance and historical and continuing importance . However , the Government breached its obligations . The rights of Maori were largely ignored for generations . Oppression of Maori voices made Maori strangers in their own lands . They were denied the opportunity to participate meaningfully in Government decision making . The impacts of colonisation continue to be felt today , through entrenched structural racism and poorer outcomes for Maori . <p> We continue to have work to do to ensure there is active partnership between the Government and Maori , consistent with the Treaty . <p> Indigenous rights <p> Under the Treaty , the Government has an active duty to protect the interests of Maori in their lands and taonga ( treasured possessions , including culture and language ) . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of other policy factors . <p> Successive governments have committed to providing a platform for new and continued relationships with iwi Maori ( Maori tribes ) . Providing redress for the historical actions and inaction of the Crown through Treaty settlements is crucial for addressing historical Treaty grievances . Treaty settlements are comprehensive agreements , with legal force , that settle all of a Maori claimant group 's historical claims against the Government . Settlements usually include a Government apology to the claimant group for the Government 's actions ( or inaction ) , and cultural , financial and commercial redress . The apology is a valuable way to help restore the mana ( esteem ) of the Government and begin to build a new partnership . <p> Sixty-one percent of Treaty settlements are now complete . While continuing to focus on remaining settlements , we are also moving to a post-settlement phase . This is why we have established a new Maori/Crown relations portfolio , Te Arawhiti meaning " the bridge " between Maori and the Crown . Te Arawhiti is aimed at fostering a healthier relationship between the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ engages with Maori . <p> The new portfolio is an acknowledgement that , although we are not there yet , we are beginning to shift our focus from the wrongs of the past , to improving outcomes for Maori for the future . The damaging effects of colonisation are still being felt today , with Maori facing considerable disadvantages . If we are to address the seemingly intractable problems facing some Maori , like the disproportionate representation of Maori in state care and in our prisons , then we need to work constructively with Maori to find solutions . <p> Structural discrimination and marginalised groups <p> We know that some New Zealanders face more barriers than others . @@70462319 <h> By asking for evidence of climate change , a council is neglecting its duty <p> A resident on the West Coast 's Buller coastline cleans up after a wave flooded her property in 2017 . <p> OPINION:The West Coast is a colourful and beautiful place , made all the more interesting by the fact it so often marches to its own political drumbeat . <p> It is the birthplace of the Labour Party , the spiritual home for anti-1080 activism , and now , the only region in the country opposing the Zero Carbon Bill , a generally uncontroversial law that has broad bipartisan support across much of the country . <p> Most of the West Coast is mature native forest in the conservation estate , meaning it has limited capacity to plant new forests to collect carbon credits ; its major industries ( particularly milk processing ) are heavily reliant on fossil fuels ; ind the region 's wobbly economy risks toppling completely if large-scale changes are imposed upon it without caution . <p> These issues merit further discussion and need to be addressed . <p> A major concern about responding to climate change is establishing what @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to ease into a low-carbon economy by minimising the damage to communities like those on the West Coast . <p> The council has undermined its perfectly valid points , however , by appearing to put the nostalgic , industry-motivated reasoning of some of its members above the threat climate change poses to the broader community . <p> It 's most obvious in one strand of its submission , which has been emphasised in the media coverage : " Climate change is a very complex issue and to ask the people of the West Coast to commit to an emissions target ... the evidence proving anthropogenic climate change must be presented and proven beyond reasonable doubt . " <p> Firstly , climate change is n't complicated . We 've known since the 19th century that certain gases absorb and re-radiate heat , and we know the concentration of those gases in the atmosphere has increased dramatically in the last century due to human activity . <p> We know temperatures are increasing because we 've been measuring them for a long time , and every long-term temperature record shows the same trend @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a reasonable doubt " is also confusing . Scientists are n't prosecuting a criminal case , which they stop once a jury has made its decision ; they continue to think , experiment , and test their hypotheses , resulting in a scientific record that swells like a balloon expanding infinitely , from which policymakers draw conclusions based on the body of evidence . <p> Decades of this process has led to overwhelming evidence that the climate is warming as the direct result of human activity . <p> An argument put forward by the submission 's author - the council 's planning , science and innovation manager Hadley Mills - does not inspire confidence that this is well understood . <p> On RNZ , he said the social and economic costs related to the Bill were n't made clear , but also suggested the science behind climate change was too complicated to understand , and the information had not been presented clearly enough . <p> IAIN MCGREGOR/STUFF <p> Ken Richards after the ocean swamped his property in Granity in 2018 . <p> " We want the science presented really simply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ staff , so we just want everyone to understand it and to be really clear and open about why we 're doing what we 're doing , " he told RNZ . <p> One of the responsibilities of a regional council is to make decisions on behalf of its constituents on technical matters . <p> That includes council staffers , as well as elected representatives . In this case , both staff and councillors have thrown up their hands and decided they 're hopelessly unable to fulfil a basic task that , somehow , every other regional council was capable of completing . <p> It 's also undermined by the fact that climate experts have spoken to the council about climate change issues , including Niwa 's Dr Rob Bell , a coastal engineering expert who co-wrote the national guidance on climate change all councils use as a reference point . <p> Even if he had n't , it 's not hard to find out more about climate change , the predominant scientific issue of our time - ignorance , in this case , is a shoddy excuse . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on a superficial level , is that two councillors in particular are known to be so-called ' climate change sceptics ' : Allan Birchfield and Neal Clementson , who both run mining companies . <p> Birchfield , in fact , made his own submission on the Zero Carbon Bill , in which he alleges without evidence that the temperature record " has been tampered with " , that there is still serious debate among scientists about the causes of climate change ( there 's not ) , and that the world is about to enter an ice age . <p> While less outspoken than his colleague , Clementson , on his Facebook page , has favourably shared information questioning the science of climate change , and told Birchfield in a council meeting in 2017 that he was " preaching to the converted " when Birchfield brought up his belief that climate change was a hoax . <p> People who still hold these views , contrary to decades of scientific evidence , are unlikely to be convinced at this point . As the saying goes , you ca n't reason someone @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> It also goes without saying that West Coasters deserve better representation . The ability to distinguish between reliable and unreliable information is a vital skill for elected officials , and in the case of these two councillors - as it is with the likes of New Conservatives member David Moffett - the issue of climate change keenly exposes this flaw in a way other issues do not . <p> But they are just two members of a seven-strong council . Another important role for elected officials is to tell their constituents the truth , and by failing to discuss and take seriously the threat climate change poses to the region , the council as a whole failed in that basic task . <p> It 's an issue in regions such as the West Coast that elected regional officials represent a time and place that may no longer exist . There are more than 120 regional councillors in New Zealand , and you can count the number that are aged under 40 on one hand . <p> That may be why mining still dominates political conversations on the West @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fourth-largest industry , contributing half of what agriculture does to its annual GDP and considerably less than tourism . <p> There are fewer than 300 coal miners left on the West Coast ( down from more than 1000 in 2012 ) , along with about 170 gold miners . @@70464066 <h> Waltzing to nowhere <p> In a speech last year , the former Secretary to the Treasury Ken Henry , now Chairman of the National Australia Bank , summed up the distressing state of policy making in Australia -- " Not so many years ago , an optimistic nation of Australians could be proud of a country that pioneered world 's best policy ... But nobody any longer looks to Australia to see how it should be done . " <p> How can he make such a claim when Australia continues to enjoy a world-beating period of uninterrupted economic growth now exceeding a quarter of a century ? Very easily . It is a classic case of the old adage -- good times make bad policy . In the economic sphere , perhaps more than in any other , Australia is resting on its laurels . It languishes in what economist Ross Garnaut calls " the great complacency " . <p> Every major policy responsible for Australia 's economic success was in place by 2001 . The last piece of substantive economic reform was the introduction of GST in 2001 . There is no better illustration of the reform @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' everything is on the table ' , substantive reform has proved impossible . Successive governments have done little more than tweak the tax rates and thresholds . ( Many Australians are curious to see what New Zealand 's Tax Working Group recommends and , more importantly , what becomes of those recommendations . ) <p> Much of Australia 's GDP growth has been driven by immigration . As in New Zealand , the GDP growth picture is much less impressive on a per capita basis , particularly over the last ten years . This is currently being experienced in the form of an extended period of stagnating wages . Journalist David Uren highlighted the reality in early 2018 -- " Australians have endured their longest period of falling living standards in more than a quarter of a century as growth in costs outstripped earnings for the fifth consecutive quarter , leaving households worse off than they were six years ago . " <p> Meanwhile , Australia is sliding down the international competitiveness rankings -- from a high of 15th in 2009-10 to 21st in 2017-18 according to the World @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ government debt has risen faster than that of almost every other advanced country . As think tank executive John Roskam pointed out in 2017 , " in 2005 only seven countries had a lower level of government debt than Australia . Now 50 countries do " . <p> Australia 's rising government debt reflects an unbroken run of federal budget deficits for the last decade . Year after year various federal Treasurers have produced a current deficit but earnestly promised surpluses just around the corner -- an eternal treadmill of disappointment . The recurring refrain from these latter-day St Augustines has been give me deficit chastity and fiscal continence , but just not yet . While light is finally appearing at the end of the tunnel , it may yet be extinguished by politicians seeking to buy the 2019 federal election with promises of tax cuts and increased government spending . <p> A decade of deficits seems both remarkable and disheartening during a period in which resource-rich Australia has experienced the greatest mining boom in its history . Compare that with Norway , another developed country that enjoys abundant natural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a US $1 trillion sovereign wealth fund . In the 2018 financial year , that fund made a profit of more than US $130 billion , equal to about a third of Norway 's GDP . By comparison , Australia has the Future Fund of just US $100 billion ( to meet US $150 billion of public sector employee superannuation liabilities ) and record government debt . <p> Policy making beyond the economy is often equally lamentable . The most crucial area for the country 's future is education . The best measure of the relative performance of Australia 's education system is the Programme for International Student Assessment ( PISA ) . Its most recent report from 2015 makes depressing reading for Australians . The average performance for 15-year olds has declined steadily over a ten year period in every subject measured -- science , mathematics , and reading . In the same subjects there has been a constant decline in the share of top performers and a constant increase in the share of low performers . <p> Indigenous affairs is another stunning example of policy failure , whether @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gap ' or the on-going debacle of constitutional recognition . The government also seems incapable of resolving the problem of the offshore detention of refugees , a problem that does more to tarnish Australia 's international reputation than any other . The National Broadband Network is a source of national embarrassment . Other countries , including New Zealand , appear able to create much faster and more reliable broadband networks at a fraction of the cost . Few things unite Australians quite like their shared hostility to the seemingly doomed NBN . <p> For pure political malfunction , nothing approaches the fiasco of Australia 's energy policy . Journalist Paul Kelly calls it " the catastrophic Australian legacy of the past decade " . With vast reserves of coal , oil , natural gas , and uranium , and limitless supplies of sun , wind , and waves , Australia ranks as one of the most energy blessed nations on earth . Wherever the policy makers stand on climate change , they should be able to ensure that Australians enjoy a reliable and affordable supply of energy . And yet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ years . <p> Australians now suffer some of the highest electricity prices in the world and an increasing risk of blackouts . According to the former Secretary to the Treasury John Fraser consultation with industry in 2017 revealed " widespread concern around how energy policy uncertainty is contributing to investment uncertainty , higher power prices and poorer system reliability " . <p> In 1964 in his book The Lucky Country , Donald Horne described Australia as " a lucky country run mainly by second rate people who share its luck " . That has not been a fair description for all of the intervening half-century but it seems depressingly appropriate today . Australia remains a great place to live in spite of its current politicians not because of them . <p> Newsroom is powered by the generosity of readers like you , who support our mission to produce fearless , independent and provocative journalism . <h> Comments <p> Newsroom does not allow comments directly on this website . @@70464069 <h> Smallpox : a disease in deep freeze <p> In the first of an ongoing series on vaccines , Farah Hancock takes a look back at the first vaccine created and the only human disease to be eradicated <p> A cow called Blossom is the unlikely hero in the fight against a disease estimated to have killed between 300 and 500 million people . <p> Smallpox is now eradicated , with the last recorded case in the 1970s . The keys to its eradication were milkmaids , cows and the development of the world 's first vaccine . <p> University of Waikato 's senior lecturer in biological sciences Alison Campbell said the disease would start with symptoms similar to a flu . <p> " You would get a really high fever , you would get headaches , you would feel like crap . Your joints would hurt . Then you would get a rash which would start off on your head and spread over your body . It started as a red rash , then it went into bumps and the bumps turned into these pussy blisters . <p> " Then the blisters burst , and you were open @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scabbed off you normally recovered . That 's some small comfort . " <p> There were four types of the smallpox disease . Overall the fatality rate was 30 percent but for haemorrhagic smallpox the death rate was nearly 100 percent . Spread through particles in the air , contact with infected material , and sometimes even bedding , smallpox infected both adults and children . <p> A Bangladeshi girl with smallpox , 1973 . <p> Smallpox is one of many diseases for which vaccines have been developed . With vaccination rates falling , there 's concern among health professionals that people have forgotten the severity of some of the diseases vaccines prevent . <p> Unless smallpox escapes from the laboratories which hold small samples of the virus , or somehow re-emerges as a result of climate change , there 's little chance it will re-establish itself . However , many other serious vaccine-preventable diseases still occur naturally in the world . <p> " 2000 came down with it , mostly Maori and there were 55 deaths , also mostly Maori . " <p> The World Health Organisation ( WHO @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2019 's top 10 threats to global health and notes there has been a 30 percent increase in measles . It worries that a hesitancy to vaccinate threatens to reverse progress made tackling vaccine-preventable diseases . <p> Another threat on the WHO 's top 10 list is antimicrobial resistance . Their website says : " Antimicrobial resistance -- the ability of bacteria , parasites , viruses and fungi to resist these medicines -- threatens to send us back to a time when we were unable to easily treat infections such as pneumonia , tuberculosis , gonorrhoea , and salmonellosis . " <p> In some cases , vaccines preventing diseases such as tuberculosis and possibly gonorrhoea could be a saving grace when antibiotics become ineffective . <p> Smallpox in New Zealand <p> Despite being separated from other countries by long sea voyages , New Zealand was not spared the disease . It killed far fewer people than influenza , but its arrival was met with strict controls in an attempt to contain it . <p> " The worst outbreak we had was in Northland in 1913 . Apparently , a missionary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a ship while he was getting out here . He went to a hui in April and spread it around , " said Campbell <p> " Two thousand came down with it , mostly Maori , and there were 55 deaths , also mostly Maori . " <p> The disease was controlled through quarantine , travel restrictions and a mass vaccination programme . <p> " Interestingly the article I read said Maori were far more willing to be vaccinated than Pakeha were . " <p> Part of the willingness may have been due to public health measures . In order to travel by train during the outbreak , Maori people were required to present a certificate to prove they had been vaccinated . <p> A certificate Maori passengers needed to present in order to travel on trains during the 1913 smallpox outbreak . Photo : CC BY 3.0 <p> Preventing the ' pox <p> The path to the vaccine was winding . Initially variolation was used . The term came from the name of the smallpox virus , variola . The practice has been documented in China , Turkey and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the 15th century , with a description that scabs were powdered and blown up the nose of a healthy person . <p> Campbell said other countries relied on breaking the skin . <p> " Some old lady usually , they tended to be the one nursing the sick people , would collect some pus from someone 's open blisters . They would go to someone who wanted to have the variolation treatment done , and they would scratch their skin until it bled with a needle , and then put some pus into the wound . <p> " Sometimes you got full-blown smallpox and died . " <p> Often though , people would get a mild form of the disease , recover and develop immunity to the virus . <p> The method was introduced to the western world by English aristocrat Lady Mary Montagu . She survived smallpox as a child but had lost other family members to the disease . While living in Turkey she learnt of variolation and in 1718 had her five-year-old son successfully variolated . <p> This was overseen by an English doctor who decided @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trial was conducted on condemned prisoners who Campbell said were given a deal " better than hanging " . <p> " If you survive , we 'll let you go . They all survived and presumably he let them go . " <p> This began the widespread acceptance of the method . However , the risk of death remained . Another serious issue was the number of variolated people spreading the disease to others while they were contagious . <p> A case of smallpox , 1886 . <p> Blossom , the milkmaid and the gardener 's son <p> At the close of the 18th Century , English physician and scientist Edward Jenner realised milkmaids seldom got smallpox . He postulated that the immunity could be due to their exposure to cowpox . Milkmaids were often exposed to cowpox by touching infected cows ' udders . Cowpox does affect humans but is far less severe than smallpox . <p> He tested his theory on his gardener 's eight-year-old son . A cow called Blossom had infected a milkmaid with cowpox . Blisters from the milkmaid 's hand were scraped and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ weeks later he exposed the boy to smallpox . <p> " The boy did n't get it . These days this would be unethical , but back in the day that was the way people worked . " <p> Subsequent tests had the same result and vaccination replaced variolation as a method which had the advantage of not killing the recipient and not causing the spread of the smallpox virus . <p> " The other fear was somebody other than the US and Russia might have a supply and they might release it as a bio-terrorism act . " <p> By the late 1800s a standardised vaccine was created and the last naturally occurring instance of the disease was recorded in Somalia in 1977 . Another death in 1978 happened when a laboratory-stored virus caused the death of a medical photographer . <p> Smallpox under lock and key <p> The disease is eradicated in the wild but is still kept in two approved laboratories in the United States and Russia . In 1986 the WHO recommended all stocks of the virus should be destroyed . There was opposition to this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is to develop better vaccines and better treatments . They have actually come up with a better vaccine than the one which was in operation , " Campbell said . <p> " The other fear was somebody other than the US and Russia might have a supply and they might release it as a bio-terrorism act . " <p> This fear was so great 450,000 US military personal were vaccinated after 9/11 . <p> Instances of the virus have been found outside of the sanctioned laboratories . In 2013 cloned fragments of the virus were found in a South African laboratory . <p> In 2014 , vials from the 1950s containing live samples of smallpox were discovered in an old cardboard box in an unused part of a storeroom of the National Institute of Health in the US . <p> In both instances the virus was destroyed under the supervision of the WHO . The question over the destruction of the remaining samples held in the approved laboratory deep freeze remains open . <p> Zombie anthrax <p> There 's a small chance the virus may resurface in the wild as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ permafrost is uncovering infected corpses . " Zombie " anthrax , caught from spores in long-dead reindeer , infected 24 people and led to a mass cull of reindeer in the region in case they had contracted it . Since then scientists have looked for for signs of smallpox in frozen corpses found in the area . <p> Corpses were found with sores resembling those caused by the virus , and fragments of the virus 's DNA have been found in one body believed date to the 1700s . The virus is known to remain viable for more than a decade in saved scabs in a temperate climate , so there 's a possibility more than just fragments may eventually be found in places where extreme cold has preserved them . <p> Whether the virus could be revived and become infectious is another question . Two " giant " viruses ( a type of virus so large they can be seen under a normal microscope ) have been found after 30,000 years under the Siberian permafrost . Posing no threat to humans as they only infect single-celled organisms , these @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Scientists , cautious as always , now rate the chance a microbe could be revived and infect humans as a non-zero probability . <p> In the event of a non-zero probability chance the virus escapes from a frozen tomb , a laboratory , or be used as a weapon , the effect on a population which has n't vaccinated for decades could be devastating . <p> Newsroom is powered by the generosity of readers like you , who support our mission to produce fearless , independent and provocative journalism . <h> Comments <p> Newsroom does not allow comments directly on this website . Labour activists and trade unions have a long history of association with trade policy and workers issues have been at the heart of the protection versus free trade arguments for time immemorial . Jobs are not the only part of our lives -- there 's kids , recreation -- but jobs are a big part of our lives . So we have an interest in issues that have a big impact on jobs . Not only the impact that trade and commercial agreements have on working and conditions for jobs , but also in terms of the wider social wage that workers experience in terms of our need for strong public services . We have looked to having some firm commitments , such as countries ' nationally determined contributions being part of trade and investment agreements , rather than the voluntary non-binding nature they currently are in the Paris Agreement . <p> So we have a wide range of interests . There 's a lot to it . @@70464518 <h> The Lancet : The drivers of obesity and climate change <p> Leaders must take a hard line against powerful commercial interests and rethink global economic incentives within the food system in order to tackle the joint pandemics of obesity , undernutrition and climate change , according to a major new report by the Lancet Commission on Obesity . Key points : * The global interplay of obesity , undernutrition and climate change represents ' The Global Syndemic ' and is the greatest threat to human and planetary health , affecting most people in every country and region. * Powerful opposition by commercial vested interests , lack of political leadership , and insufficient societal demand for change are preventing action on The Global Syndemic , with rising rates of obesity and greenhouse gas emissions , and stagnating rates of undernutrition. * New social movement for change and radical rethink of the relationship between policymakers , business , governance and civil society is urgently needed . * The Commission calls for a global treaty to limit the political influence of Big Food ( a proposed Framework Convention on Food Systems -- modelled on global conventions on tobacco and climate change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from harmful products and towards sustainable alternatives ; and advocacy from civil society to break decades of policy inertia.University of Auckland article : https : **39;1267;TOOLONG ... Leaders must take a hard line against powerful commercial interests and rethink global economic incentives within the food system in order to tackle the joint pandemics of obesity , undernutrition and climate change , according to a major new report by the Lancet Commission on Obesity . A key recommendation from the Commission is the call to establish a new global treaty on food systems to limit the political influence of Big Food . <p> Malnutrition in all its forms , including undernutrition and obesity , is by far the biggest cause of ill-health and premature death globally . Both undernutrition and obesity are expected to be made significantly worse by climate change 1 . <p> The report follows the publication ( 17 Jan ) of the Lancet-EAT Commission , which provided the first scientific targets for a healthy diet within planetary boundaries 2 . Now , the new report analyses the wider systems underpinning the global obesity pandemic , and identifies solutions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ past two decades , obesity , undernutrition and climate change have been viewed as separate , and policy responses have been unacceptably slow due to reluctance of policy makers to implement effective policies , powerful opposition by vested commercial interests , and insufficient demand for change by the public and civil society . Undernutrition is declining too slowly to meet global targets , no country has reversed its obesity epidemic , and comprehensive policy responses to the threat of climate change have barely begun . <p> " Until now , undernutrition and obesity have been seen as polar opposites of either too few or too many calories . In reality , they are both driven by the same unhealthy , inequitable food systems , underpinned by the same political economy that is single-focused on economic growth , and ignores the negative health and equity outcomes . Climate change has the same story of profits and power ignoring the environmental damage caused by current food systems , transportation , urban design and land use . Joining the three pandemics together as The Global Syndemic allows us to consider common drivers and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy inertia , " says Commission co-chair , Professor Boyd Swinburn of the University of Auckland . 3 <p> Led by the University of Auckland ( New Zealand ) , the George Washington University ( USA ) , and World Obesity Federation ( UK ) , the new Lancet Commission is the result of a three-year project led by 43 experts from a broad range of expertise from 14 countries 4 . <p> The new Commission defines The Global Syndemic as the global interactions of the pandemics of obesity , undernutrition and climate change , which are linked through common drivers and shared solutions . Driving The Global Syndemic are food and agriculture policies , transportation , urban design and land use systems - which in turn are driven by policies and economic incentives that promote overconsumption and inequalities . <p> Among the actions recommended , the Commission calls for the establishment of a Framework Convention on Food Systems ( FCFS ) - similar to global conventions for tobacco control and climate change -- to restrict the influence of the food industry in policy making and to mobilise national action @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Economic incentives must be redesigned , and US$ 5 trillion in government subsidies to fossil fuel and large agricultural businesses globally should be redirected towards sustainable , healthy , environmentally friendly activities . Additionally , a global philanthropic fund of US$1 billion must be set up to support civil society in advocating for change . <p> " The prevailing business model of large international food and beverage companies that focus on maximising short-term profits leads to overconsumption of nutrient-poor food and beverages in both high-income countries and increasingly in low and middle-income countries . The coexistence of obesity and stunting in the same children in some countries is an urgent warning signal -- and both will be exacerbated by climate change . Tackling The Global Syndemic requires an urgent rethink of how we eat , live , consume , and move , including a radical change to a sustainable and health-promoting business model fit for the future challenges we face today , " says Dr Richard Horton , Editor-in-Chief , The Lancet . 3 <p> The Global Syndemic : common drivers require shared solutions <p> The Global Syndemic represents a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interact with each other , and share common underlying societal drivers . For example , food systems not only drive the obesity and undernutrition pandemics but also generate 25-30% of greenhouse gas emissions ( GHGs ) , and cattle production accounts for over half of those . Car-dominated transportation systems support sedentary lifestyles and generate between 14-25% of GHGs . Underpinning all of these are weak political governance systems , the unchallenged economic pursuit of GDP growth , and the powerful commercial engineering of overconsumption . <p> " We must recognise these connections and implement double-duty actions that address both obesity and undernutrition and triple-duty actions that influence multiple parts of the syndemic simultaneously , " says Commissioner Professor Corinna Hawkes , City University London ( UK ) 3 . Guidelines for a sustainable diet , the restriction of commercial influences , the right to wellbeing legislation , and policies for healthy , equitable , environmentally sustainable , economically prosperous food systems would all have an impact across obesity , undernutrition and climate change ( ie , triple-duty , or triple-win actions ) . Additional examples would include : <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , health and environmental labelling , and social marketing would lead to healthier diets for cancer and obesity prevention , more land for efficient , sustainable agriculture , providing opportunities to reduce undernutrition , and lower GHG emissions from agriculture . <p> * Supporting active transportation through infrastructure , taxes and subsidy shifts , and social marketing strategies would lead to increased physical activity and less sedentary time , with an impact on obesity prevention , cheaper transport access to healthy food and employment , potentially reducing poverty and undernutrition , and lower GHG emissions from transportation . <p> Commercial vested interests : a powerful driver of The Global SyndemicEconomic power has been increasingly concentrated into fewer , larger companies . Key strategies used by the food industry to obstruct obesity prevention policies have included adopting self-regulation to pre-empt or delay state regulation , public relations efforts portraying industry as socially responsible while undermining and contesting the strength of scientific evidence , direct lobbying of government decision-makers , and framing nutrition as a matter of individual responsibility . <p> " With market power comes political power , and even willing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ New governance dynamics are needed to break the policy inertia preventing action . Governments need to regain the power to act in the interests of people and the planet and global treaties help to achieve this . Vested commercial interests need to be excluded from the policy table , and civil society needs to have a stronger voice in policy-making . @@70467224 <p> Local councils are facing a $5-8 billion bill to replace vital infrastructure lost to climate change in the next half-century - and they want a national war chest to pay for it . <p> For the first time , environment and engineering researchers have calculated the cost of replacing pipes , roads and buildings destroyed by sea-level rise . <p> The data is included in a new Local Government New Zealand report which spells out a dire warning about the country 's ability to fund repairs . The organisation is now calling on the Government to create a national climate change adaptation fund to help meet the costs . <p> IAIN MCGREGOR/STUFF <p> Coastal settlements - like Southshore and New Brighton - have been earmarked as being at risk of sea level rise . <p> " This moment will not come again ... we may estimate a window of roughly 25 years before government starts parking its ambulance at the bottom of a metaphorical hill , " the report says . <p> LGNZ advocates for the interests of local authorities . It commissioned the Tonkin and Taylor study to determine how much infrastructure is exposed to sea level @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The data was collected by surveying 60 councils on roads ; drinking , waste and storm water ( known as ' three waters ' ) ; infrastructure ; and buildings . They also looked at green space , jetties and airports . The report does not extend to central government infrastructure and private property . <p> They considered four scenarios : 0.5 metres of sea level rise , 1m , 1.5m and 3m . NASA scientists predict a rise of between 30cm and 1.3m by 2100 . NIWA estimates between 40 centimetres and roughly 1 metre . <p> This study highlights that in the next 50 to 75 years , replacing local government infrastructure damaged by sea level rise alone could cost between $5 billion and $8 billion . <p> " This is a minimum baseline figure and does not include other costs resulting from increased flooding or drought , " the report says . " Costs will likely go far beyond tangible measures ; not only will infrastructure be exposed , but so will potential economic development and growth , community health and safety and social support systems . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cost of replacing all exposed infrastructure would be approximately $8b . That includes 6000 kilometres of pipe - roughly equivalent to the distance of a return trip from Melbourne to Darwin - and more than 2000 km of road . More than 2000 buildings and facilities across the country are also at risk . <p> At this level , Canterbury 's exposure is the greatest , followed by the Hawke 's Bay and by Auckland . <p> If waves head towards 3m , the cost rises above $15b . <p> For context , gross domestic product ( GDP ) is just over $300b . The rebuild following the Canterbury earthquakes was estimated to cost upwards of $40b and the South Canterbury Finance bailout was $1.6b . <p> The figures do not include the cost of temporary or permanent adaptation measures , planning or buying other resources to ensure acceptable levels of service . <p> THREE WATERS <p> Replacing all the exposed council-owned ' three waters ' infrastructure - such as pipes , pump stations , manholes and treatment plants - will cost more than the combined cost of restoring roads @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> At half a metre , the report estimates replacement will cost $1.4b . At 1m metre , the value is $2.6b , soaring to $4b at 1.5m and by 3m it will cost over $7bn . At a minimum , that works out as more than $540 per person if the sea rises by 1m . <p> Hawke 's Bay , Bay of Plenty , Waikato and Auckland have the largest totals of exposed assets . <p> But , given the South Island has just 25 per cent of the population , ratepayers there face the highest costs per capita . Canterbury holds the most exposed water assets , including 650 kilometres of water pipes and over 120 pump stations . <p> Those costs could blow out further - the estimates also do n't factor in salt water intrusion into aquifers , and investment to draw freshwater from new places . <p> The study indicates around 2100km of sealed and unsealed roads will be exposed up to the 1.5m increment , with a replacement value of $1b . For roads exposed to 3m of inundation , the analysis expects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The estimates do not include bridges . <p> In the North Island , the at-risk areas total between 380km and 2860km , with the Hawke 's Bay and Bay of Plenty bearing the highest costs . Further south it is Otago , Canterbury and Tasman roads which will bear the brunt . <p> The report notes : " The difference in impacts and costs will be dramatic for South Island councils in the near term . Further , critical coastal infrastructure drawing tourism will be deeply impacted , potentially affecting local economic productivity and business development . " <p> It recommends enhanced long term planning , prioritising " lifeline " roads , as well as discussing alternatives and costs with locals and businesses . <p> BUILDINGS <p> The survey collected data on community facilities , council housing , council offices , and other significant buildings . <p> Nationally , with a 0.5m sea level rise , approximately 780 council-owned buildings will be exposed , costing $200m . <p> At the 1.0m elevation , that rises to 1400 buildings , costing $780m . It also stores heat-trapping carbon dioxide deep in the ocean . <p> The faster it moves , the more warm water gets sent into the depths to cool . <p> The area where warm water turns over in the North Atlantic is considered to be the engine of the conveyor belt . <p> But then a new international science team measured temperature , saltiness and the speed of ocean currents throughout the North Atlantic to try to better understand the conveyor belt . <p> The preliminary results after hundreds of measurements in 21 months found that engine was several hundreds of kilometres east of where they figured , said study lead author Susan Lozier , an ocean sciences professor at Duke University . <p> The study , published in Thursday 's journal Science , puts it east of Greenland , closer to Scotland . <p> The computer simulations that predict how the climate could change in coming years did n't factor in exactly where the conveyor belt engine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Lozier and several outside experts said this did n't change their trust in the models , especially because when the models are checked with what is happening in the real world , they are found to be generally accurate . <p> " It does n't mean that the models are all wrong at all , " said Tom Delworth , a senior scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 's geophysical lab in Princeton , New Jersey . <p> MIT 's Carl Wunsch and other outside experts said the study was helpful , but pointed out that 21 months of study is not enough to know if this different location is temporary or permanent . <p> Scientists have long feared that the conveyor belt could be slowing and , in a worst-case scenario , could even stop and cause abrupt and catastrophic climate change . <p> It is considered a potential climate tipping point that was the premise of the scientifically inaccurate 2004 disaster movie The Day After Tomorrow . <p> Based on computer model studies , the United Nations ' Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reported in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the conveyor belt would collapse this century . <p> But the Nobel Prize-winning scientific panel concluded it is likely to get about a third slower if greenhouse gas emissions continue at its current pace . <p> A study last year found that global warming is weakening the system , saying the conveyor belt was moving at its slowest speed in nearly 140 years of records . <p> " Our basic understanding that the collapse is unlikely still stands , " said Delworth , who was n't part of the study .

@@70472131 <h> Has the corporate bond market partied too hard ? <h> Financial markets over the last few years have enjoyed the equivalent of a " long hot summer " characterised by calm weather and warm sunny days . From experience , we all know that long hot summer days can occasionally encourage excess in the form of too much sun or fun . The same excess is also a risk for financial markets and the wider economy . <h> Friday , February 1st 2019 , 8:00AM <p> by Mark Brooks <p> Mark Brooks <p> Locally the good times are obvious in the number of cranes on the skylines of our major cities and in the difficulty of finding staff . The United States is also seeing similar capacity constraints as labour market surveys show there are more job openings than there are unemployed . <p> There is a saying that financial bull markets do not die of old age . Instead , they end due to a combination of capacity shortages constraining growth and central banks increasing interest rates to counter the risk of rising inflation . <p> In the United States this process in now well under way @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ already and will probably do so again in December . Higher interest rates have tightened monetary conditions in the United States and globally . This squeezes those in a weaker position , primarily those with excessive debt loads and/or economically sensitive incomes . During the Global Financial Crisis this was predominately households in the United States and in New Zealand , non-bank lenders such as finance companies . <p> This time round , a key area of stress is likely to be the corporate bond market . A decade of ultra-low interest rates forced many investors out of cash as it did not generate a return into other investment assets . Much of this money flowed into the corporate bond market . Globally , companies were more than happy to accommodate this demand by issuing bonds at historically low interest rates . In the United States , this has seen the corporate bond market double in size over the past decade to more than $5 trillion . <p> Initially the bond issuance was used to replace higher cost debt with cheaper funding but as the cycle continued , companies have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fund the purchase of their own shares . Excessive buybacks can leave a company with more debt to repay and no new sources of revenue with which to repay it . Many of the bonds used to fund buybacks have been issued by companies at the lower end of the investment grade spectrum : BBB rated bonds rather than A rated bonds ( BB , B and CCC rated bonds are not considered investment grade ) . BBB rated bonds now account for over 48% of the United States investment grade bond universe , up from 34% at their low 10 years ago . <p> The pattern in New Zealand is different as we have not seen companies increase their debt levels to the same degree . However , companies have increasingly issued bonds to replace bank debt , issue subordinated debt and remove investor friendly terms from their bond documents . This makes these bonds more exposed to any slowing in the economy . In a slowing economy the combination of declining earnings and rising debt costs will see interest coverage erode and make the BBB investment grade bond @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for many investors will be to sell these bonds . This can be more challenging for bonds . Unlike shares , the secondary market for bonds is limited and this is especially true in New Zealand . It is easy to buy a bond when it is first issued , but more difficult to sell the same bond before it matures . We therefore anticipate the markets may struggle to absorb this selling without a significant re-pricing . In anticipation of this , we have substantially reduced clients ' exposure to lower quality investment grade bonds and have invested in downside mitigation strategies that are designed to limit the impact of a downturn in investment grade bonds . <p> * Source : International Monetary Fund . Barclays Capital . Tse Capital . <p> Mark Brooks is Head of Income at New Zealand Funds Management Limited ( NZ Funds ) . @@70472485 <h> Nutrient Management and Waitaki Plan Change operative <p> Environment Canterbury has announced that the Nutrient Management and Waitaki Plan Change , Plan Change 5 to the Land &amp; Water Regional Plan , is operative from today , 1 February 2019 . <p> Councillor Peter Skelton said this was the final step in a three-year process setting industry agreed " Good Management Practice " as the minimum standard for all farming activities . <p> " The plan change deals with the effects of land uses , particularly farming activities , on water quality at a region-wide level , and ensures the effective management of water quality in the Waitaki sub-region , " Professor Skelton said . <p> The nutrient management rules apply in all catchments in the region not currently the subject of sub-region plans . <p> " Resource consent , including audited Farm Environment Plans , is required if properties irrigate more than 50 hectares or have more than a specified amount of winter grazing of cattle , depending on property size , " Professor Skelton said . <p> " The nutrient management rules are intended to address the effects of changing land use and promote improved water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in mind , we need to be clear about what constitutes Good Management Practice on farm . " This is a requirement for farms requiring land use consent to farm , " Professor Skelton said . " Permitted farms need only comply with the irrigation and winter grazing limits . " <p> As part of the process to settle appeals on the plan change , an external working group was established to consider some implementation challenges . " I am confident that this work will achieve both of these outcomes and I thank the working group for its efforts . <p> " Excellent progress has been made with our planning work in the last few years , " Peter Skelton concluded . @@70472494 <h> Protecting New Zealand 's Threatened Wetlands <p> The public is being encouraged to buy a specially commissioned wildlife habitat stamp to mark World Wetlands Day , with funds raised from sales being used to protect New Zealand 's fast-disappearing natural habitat . <p> World Wetlands Day is celebrated around the globe on February 2 to mark the 1971 signing of the Convention on Wetlands - the Ramsar Convention . <p> This year 's theme is " wetlands and climate change " which is aimed at raising awareness about the continuing drainage of wetlands and spark action to stop the destruction . <p> Wetlands are among the world 's most threatened habitats and in New Zealand , more than 90 percent of them have been destroyed . <p> Fish and Game is one of New Zealand 's major defenders of wetlands and is urging New Zealanders to help protect these vital but fast-diminishing habitats by buying the latest Habitat Trust stamp . <p> Fish and Game policy manager Robert Sowman oversees the stamp programme which he says has made a valuable contribution to protecting wetlands since the first stamp was released a quarter of a century ago . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to protect , enhance and create wetlands and other wildlife habitat around the country , " Mr Sowman says . <p> The stamps are compulsory for all game bird hunters to buy so their hunting licences are valid . <p> Robert Sowman says while the programme is a powerful example of hunters ' commitment to conservation , anyone including non-hunters can buy one . <p> " Any New Zealander supporting conservation and wanting to see wildlife habitat protected can buy a stamp , knowing that the money raised will have a lasting impact . <p> " Native birds , fish and plants all benefit from habitat stamp sales . Last year alone , we distributed tens of thousands of dollars towards protecting , creating and enhancing habitat thanks to the revenue we earned from these sales , " Mr Sowman says . <p> " Most of these grants are made to private property owners including farmers , although financial support is also given to big projects , such as Marlborough 's Para Wetlands which will be familiar to anyone travelling the road between Blenheim and Picton .
